items.title: Each of your sperm/eggs is one of 2 to the 23rd power possibilities
items.claim: Meiosis shuffles 23 chromosome pairs into 23 gametes. From you alone, ignoring recombination, that's 8.4 million possible combinations. Add crossing over and the count is effectively infinite. Why is sexual reproduction so expensive to maintain?
items.prompt: Why has sex (rather than cloning) persisted in almost all eukaryotes?

options.text: Sex is uniformly better than cloning

Sex generates genetic variation that helps populations adapt to changing environments (the Red Queen hypothesis: ongoing host-parasite arms races favour variability); also recombination weeds out accumulated harmful mutations more efficiently than clonal lineages can
Sex is necessary for cell division

items.reveal_title: The twofold cost and the Red Queen
items.reveal:
A sexually reproducing female passes 50 percent of her genes to each offspring. An asexual female passes 100 percent. Asexual lineages should outcompete sexual ones by a factor of two each generation. They mostly don't.

Leading explanations:
- Red Queen (Hamilton, Van Valen): parasites and pathogens evolve to attack common host genotypes; sexual reproduction keeps host genotypes shifting so parasites can't catch up.
- Muller's ratchet: asexual lineages accumulate harmful mutations and cannot purge them efficiently. Recombination lets harmful mutations be separated from beneficial ones.
- Fisher-Muller: sex can combine beneficial mutations from different lineages.

Observationally, almost all asexual lineages are evolutionarily young, suggesting they accumulate problems and go extinct.
items.why: Sex's costs are enormous and obvious; its benefits are subtle and long-term. Evolution favours it anyway, and the reasons are still debated.

items.title: Eyes have evolved independently more than 40 times
items.claim: Eyes are complicated. Darwin worried about them in Origin of Species. Modern phylogenetics shows that eyes — from basic photoreceptors to full image-forming structures — have evolved independently somewhere between 40 and 60 times across animal lineages.
items.prompt: What does this tell us about evolution?

options.text: Eyes are too complex to evolve once, let alone many times

Photoreception is selected for so strongly that wherever a workable starting point exists (a light-sensitive protein) selection assembles eyes; complex outcomes evolve repeatedly when the gradient of advantage is steep
All eyes descend from a single ancestor
Vision is impossible without divine design

items.reveal_title: Eyes as evolutionary stress-tests for gradualism
items.reveal:
Modern eyes include: vertebrate camera eyes, cephalopod camera eyes (independently evolved, no blind spot), trilobite calcite-lens compound eyes, scallop mirror eyes, copepod parabolic-reflector eyes, jumping-spider sharp-focus eyes, brittle-star whole-body lensed skin.

Nilsson and Pelger (1994) modelled the evolution of a vertebrate-style camera eye from a flat patch of photoreceptors. With realistic mutation rates and selection coefficients of 1 percent, they estimated 400,000 generations — about half a million years — to produce a fully functional eye.

The common element across all 40+ origins: opsin proteins. The receptor molecules are conserved; the architectures around them have been built and rebuilt many times.
items.why: Eyes feel like such complex organs that they 'must' be hard to evolve. They are exactly the kind of thing selection invents many times when given a good starting molecule.

items.title: Sea otters maintain entire underwater forests
items.claim: Where sea otters live, kelp forests thrive. Where they have been hunted to near-extinction, sea urchins explode and graze kelp to bare rock ('urchin barrens'). One otter eats about 25% of its body mass in urchins daily.
items.prompt: What makes otters a keystone species?

options.text: They are the largest predators present
They selectively eat sea urchins, the only major kelp grazer in the system; removing otters releases urchin populations, which devastate kelp forests that support hundreds of other species
Otters fertilise the water with their waste

items.reveal:
Jim Estes and John Palmisano (1974) compared Aleutian islands with otters to islands where otters had been wiped out for the fur trade. The contrast was startling: lush kelp forests vs barren urchin-grazed rock.

Kelp forests are enormously productive. They support fish, invertebrates, sea birds, marine mammals. They sequester carbon. They dampen wave energy and protect coasts.

Subsequent work (Estes et al. 1998) suggested that killer whale predation on sea otters — possibly because their normal prey, large whales, had been depleted by whaling — was driving a SECOND collapse of Aleutian otter populations, with knock-on collapses of kelp.

A whaling-era extinction cascade may still be propagating decades later. Ecosystems have memory.

The 'keystone species' concept (Paine 1969) was based on starfish; otters became its most famous illustration. Many ecosystems have keystones; identifying them before they collapse is a recurring conservation challenge.
items.why: Big effects from one species seem improbable. In sea otter ecosystems, the entire architecture depends on one mid-sized predator preventing one herbivore from grazing the forest down.
